utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-17/1-T, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Furundzija, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Appearances as before?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed they are, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President. Your Honours, good morning. Defence counsel, good morning. Dr. Mujezinovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just have a few further questions for you relating to the time after the 19th of May when you had left the Vitez area. Did you re-establish any contacts as a member of the war presidency after you had left the area, after the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: After I left Vitez, I was requested, as the President of the war presidency, that is the Muslim side of the Vitez municipality, to make contact with representatives of the SDA and representatives of the military command of the BH army and to start negotiations with the Croatian side, which I refused because my family at that time was still in Vitez and they were harassed by the members of the military wing of the HVO. So I requested that my family move out from Vitez. My wife has remained in Vitez, three children, and my parents, my in-laws. My wife had a telephone, and she was enabled by the civilian police in Vitez to make one call per day. She complained of a number of provocations, break-ins, an attempt of rape in front of the children and her parents, and this was the reason why I refused to negotiate; that is, as long as my children, my wife, and my in-laws were still in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, were they, in fact, removed from Vitez, your family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR representatives went to fetch my family on two occasions, and once they were visited by the Red Cross, the International Red Cross; however, they did not manage to get them out. But finally, they were removed -- that is, they were exchanged for some Croat families who lived in Zenica and who wanted to go to Vitez. I had received a list of families which I was supposed to take back from Zenica to Vitez. Many of them didn't want to go, and I had quite a few problems because of that. Anyway, my family was eventually exchanged. It happened at the end of May 1993. And after that, in the first half of June, I became involved in negotiations with the Croat side at the British base of UNPROFOR in Stari Bila near Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you tell me, Doctor, please, who took part in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR organised negotiations, together with European monitors. I was representing the Muslim side alongside with Munib Kajmovic and the commander of the 725th brigade, it's a local Vitez brigade; and the other side, it was Mr. Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak, Maric, Josip Maric, and Joso Grbic who represented the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, how many times did you hold such negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I told you that initially I refused in May, but in June, I took part in negotiations on only one occasion because we couldn't manage to agree on some strategic points, and at that level, the negotiations were stopped. At the time, the negotiations were conducted on several levels, but I no longer took part in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that these were described as peace negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say you've taken part in just one. After that negotiation in June -- one moment, Doctor. After that negotiation in June, were the respective armed forces still in their lines, as you recalled them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had there been any general freedom of movement during that period for civilian people within Vitez or elsewhere in the region?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honours. I believe he's testified that he's in Zenica at this time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May 19th? I don't see what foundation he has laid to establish what type of freedom of movement there was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I need not pursue that question. It's really of small import. I won't cause an argument of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long did the war presidency remain in existence, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The war presidency existed, that is, was operative, operative until October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Except for -- I do apologise. I have no further questions in open session. There is one point in respect of which I would like to go into closed session, if you would be so kind, Ma'am?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The court will rise for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are in open session. Yes, Mr. Misetic, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, may it please the court. Good morning; good morning, council; good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you began your direct examination by stating that you were a party member of the SDA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you state again for us what official positions you had within the party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, I didn't have any official function within the SDA and in the first half of '91 as well. It was only in the month of September that I was elected vice-president of the executive board of the SDA branch for Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you a document which we will hand to the registrar to be marked as Defence number 1. I'd ask you to take a look at that document and see whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are there copies for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, really during our trials if you could endeavour to give copies in English translated by the official organ and also enough numbers, three of us plus --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I've been trying to figure out the technical procedures here, and I apologise for the lack of copies. But I just recently received these documents and I didn't have time to have them translated by the registry. I just asked them to authenticate it and I'll read them, if necessary, as to what they are and have the translators translate them. For the purposes of translation to the court, the top line says: "Decision on the election of the vice-president of the Vitez SDA. The following are elected vice-presidents of the SDA branch in Vitez. (1) Ahmic Mehmed, (2) Muhamed Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I do. It was signed by the president of SDA in Vitez, Mr. Munib Kajnovic. I recognised his signature. Perhaps I was not quite accurate. In the latter half of 1991, I was not actively involved, but I did confirm that I had been elected the vice-president of the SDA in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse my interruption at this stage, Your Honours, may interrupt or impose with one, it's not so much an objection to this particular document, its contents are not that contentious. I'm concerned at the practise of counsel using a language which some others in this court do not understand and then going through interpreters and reading from documents we don't understand because it could create simply that which counsel wishes to portray from a document that only he understands. I think whatever comes before the court should go through a process, at least, whereby we all are working from a commonly understood and agreed quality and level of understanding in a language of the Tribunal. As I say, I don't formally object to this document. It's only confirming a fact which the witness has already stated. It's not contentious but I think that practise is contentious and I would ask you to rule upon it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. I agree with counsel. It is not my intention to continue with the practise. This is just because I recently came into possession of these documents. In the future, I will endeavour to have them translated as fast as possible and used for the court. But rather than call the witness back at some future time to authenticate the documents, I thought I would expedite it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How many more such documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And one more document, and these are just a list of names which translation wouldn't change the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, it is taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think it is. Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, I'd like to show the witness Defence Exhibit number 2 and ask him to authenticate it. I have four copies. Again, I apologise, Your Honour, for not having the fifth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at that document, Mr. Witness? Again, I will read it. The top line says: "List of nominees to the municipal assembly of Vitez, the Party for Democratic Action, Vitez." Sir, were these the list of nominees on October 10, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a list of possible councilmen representing SDA on the municipal assembly in Vitez for the elections that took place in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you please took at number 24 on the list?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question: Is the document authentic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm just wondering, is this document an -- do you have an original document you're putting or it's just a photocopy? I just wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a copy. I'm asking the witness to authenticate it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I told you I was not active in the party in SDA so I can neither deny it nor confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: ... for the elections in 1990? [Note: First part of question obliterated by translation.]

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but I did ask them not to rank me first on the list or amongst the first because I was not interested. Well, I was nominated --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Although you were not a candidate in the party, you were not active in the party; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Quite. I made a statement sometime in August or September 1990, SDA for Vitez, but I did not actively participate in the work. I became its member but I was not active there. And the executive board of SDA proposed various candidates, and I knew I figured on this list, but I had asked them to put me somewhere towards the end of the list because, at the time, I was very busy. I wasn't really politically active, and I thought that the things would move in a completely different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it your position that although you were a candidate for the party SDA in the elections of 1990, you were not an active member of the party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't working actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may interpose, Your Honours. This line of questioning started with the authentication of a document. I suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which the witness replied to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- The authentication of the document, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, he said he can't say either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then I'm content if that has been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on your direct examination yesterday, you testified as to the formation of a Council for the Defence of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us again when that council was established and when it broke up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The council was set up on the 12th of July, '92 and was operational until, I should say, until about the establishment of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When was that? When was the war presidency established again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What exactly was your role in the Council for the Defence of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was responsible for the organisation of medical service for all the health care system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Overall, though, what did the council did? What was its purpose? What were its objectives? Was it a form of shadow government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: At the time we considered as a consultative body to the legal authorities elected in 1990 and individuals who joined that coordinating Council for the Defence of Muslims were responsible each for a particular area or a particular sphere of activity in Vitez and were to inform, to supply the media with information about the situation with the Muslims, about the position of the Muslims, individual cases and for the municipality at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then on the 15th of January, 1993, the war presidency is established. When did you become elected president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was nominated as the president of the presidency and I accepted that post on the 2nd of February, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what the war presidency did; what were its functions? Was it a form of shadow government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not a shadow government. It was a genuine government of the Muslim people under wartime conditions. It was the highest ranking body which issued orders, communications and conclusions and commanded the army, the police and everything else. So it was the supreme body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have the authority to issue orders directly to the military, the army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The military, the army in BiH -- in Vitez and the police in Vitez were not allowed to do anything without my authorisation and the authorisation of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is: Could you issue an order directly to the army?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Directly? Yes, indirectly, but only with the consent of all the members of the war presidency. I could not do it alone and I signed -- I was the one who signed the decisions of the war presidency, and the commander of the Vitez Brigade was also a member of the war presidency and that brigade was made of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who made up the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the war presidency were individuals from other parties, representatives of other parties, of Muslims in Vitez, the commander of the civilian defence, the commander of the army in Vitez. I can give you the names, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: So I was the president, and members were Asim Sivro, the representative of the liberal party, that's what is called now; Suad Salkic, an engineer from Vitez, represented the reformist party; Enes Surkovic represented the SDP; Fuad Zeco, the ternary doctor from Vitez that was the commander of the civilian defence in Vitez; and Esad Dananovic he was the commander of the local Vitez brigade; and Munib Kajnovic was the president of the SDA. Excuse me, Fuad Kakjno, the president of the Vitez government. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to apologise to you because the name of the commander of the Civil Defence, I didn't catch that. Could you repeat that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Fuad Zeco, the ternary doctor from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what the Civil Defence was? What were its functions; what did it do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Must I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The Civil Defence in Vitez was to look after the civilian population, the materiel resources, prevent accidents, rescue people, children, women, cattle in case of the danger of war. That was under the orders of the war presidency, so they were to take care of the local civilian population, their accommodation and all the matters bearing on the life of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would they also bury the dead?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time while I was in Vitez, the local population, and that was the custom there, did it, and a civilian defence was included in this; that is, every family buried their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Enes Surkovic. Could you tell us who he was, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Enes Surkovic was a teacher in the secondary school in Vitez, a mechanical engineer. On the war presidency, he represented the league of communists, the party for democratic changes, and he was a councilman and he was a councilman in the assembly elected in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did he have a particular function --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Not "Shurkavic," he is Surkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Not me, the translator?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's what it says on the monitor, "Enis Shurkavic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How long did you known Enes Surkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. -- I met Mr. Enes Surkovic when I came to work in Vitez as the teacher at the secondary school centre, and he was married to a Vitez woman, a family whom I knew who were in the indigenous population in Vitez. But he was not born in Vitez, I think he was born somewhere in Konjic, and I knew him since 1979, as a teacher. I knew him rather well because we were meeting there because of some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that during the April conflict that at one time you had to go down and find people to form a part of your negotiating team. Do you recall that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was Enes Surkovic also one of the individuals that was also part of that negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. No -- yes, he was in the cellar, in the basement, that is, he was with that group of people who when Mr. Cerkez described that group he said there was about 300 of them. I think that Enes Surkovic was one of them but I do not think that he was on the negotiating team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to refer you to a witness statement that you gave, I believe, to the Office of the Prosecutor. It is the -- if the court would indulge me for a moment until I find it. I'd like to show the witness this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When was it recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not dated on the first page. It says Sunday, 16th July on the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 1995, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you first to turn to page 10 of the statement. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you see the witness acknowledgement on that page?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you turn to page 8 now, please? On that long paragraph on that page, towards the bottom, the fourth sentence from the bottom. I'll read it and ask you to tell me whether you made that statement: "An example of the Croatian attitude is that instead of releasing people from the cellar they were sent to another prison in Busovaca, 15 of them. Some of these people were the prominent people and intellectuals. I chose to be part of the negotiating team such as Kaknjo Fuad, Sivro Bahtija, Surkovic Enes; Salkic Suad, Basic Alija, Dzidic Kadir." Was that your statement on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: See, I did not state that. I do not know English. I did state that eminent people were taken away and I said among them, there were also some who were on the negotiating team with me. These are Fuad Kaknjo, Bahtija Sivro, Kadir Dzidic. They were part of the negotiating team but what I said then was that eminent personalities were taken away, and amongst them were also some who participated in the negotiations with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me just clarify something for you. You said you don't speak English. The witness acknowledgement says that, "This Statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Was the statement read back to you in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that it was read to me, but my statement was, as I have just said, that eminent personalities, prominent personalities from Vitez were taken away, and those who were negotiating together with me, and here I think things are simply mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was it read back to you in Bosnian or wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly. It could have been read to me, but I'm telling you what my statement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you are, in fact, acknowledging that it was read back to you in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was interpreted to me in Bosnian, just as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But it was read back to you in Bosnian; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think he's already answered that question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He is equivocating. If it was read back to him in Bosnian, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Yes" or "No," sir. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was interpreted for me into Bosnian but within that context that I have just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: ... but we can move on if you answer "Yes" or "No." Was the statement read back to you in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will ask you again if you will answer "Yes" or "No." That was: The statement that I read back to you from page 8, that was a statement that you made to the interviewer; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, except that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: -- I'm repeating what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That statement makes reference, sir, to the fact that Enes Surkovic, among the other people that you name there, were taken to a prison in Busovaca. Was that statement true when you made it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Enes Surkovic spent a while in Busovaca. At the time, I was working in Vitez from the, I think, 18th, 19th of April until the 19th of May, and I had no direct contact with anyone. But Mr. Petkovic, that is, the commander of HVO, and Sefer Halilovic, who was the commander of the BiH army, visited Vitez, and I was told that it had been agreed to calm down the situation and that all the prisoners would be released. A child brought me a piece of paper to the surgery and told me that these were accommodated at the chess club, that they were singled out and put up in the chess club in Vitez, and later I learned that they had been taken to Busovaca. I do not know when they were released from Busovaca exactly, but the fact is that Mr. Surkovic spent some time in Busovaca. I had contact with him later because a member of the war presidency (sic) and he showed me a certificate issued to him by the International Red Cross that he was a released internee -- a released detainee from the prison in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You talked to him in Zenica, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what his role was in the war presidency after you and he arrived in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: His specific assignment within the war presidency included, among other things, because of a great number of people who had been expelled from Vitez, there were about four and a half thousand refugees in Zenica, in Travnik maybe 500, so his role was to coordinate with the commander of the Civil Defence and to find accommodation for these people. So he made contact with the local authorities in Zenica so that some kind of accommodation would be found for these people. He was supposed to take care of these refugees. This was the specific assignment that was given to him by the war presidency, one of the assignments that he had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about his other assignments, but first I would like to ask you: Was his responsibility, because he was a member of the war presidency, for the refugees in Zenica and in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He represented the war presidency as the person in charge of all Muslims who had been expelled from Vitez. He had his associates with whom he worked at the time. Therefore, he was also in charge for people in Travnik through his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who he worked with in Travnik, who his associates were in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that, as far as I can remember, it was Sead Cajnic, Professor Sulejman Kolasimac --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam President, I would ask that we go into closed session for a moment before the witness gives an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified yesterday that the people in the health centre told you about the events in Ahmici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You never saw those events yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You also testified that the people in the health centre, at least one of them, kissed you when she saw you because she thought you were dead. Why did they think you were dead?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is something you should ask her, really. All I know is that they read the news that I had been killed, and apparently I was the only one alive from that list that was read out on the Sarajevo TV, and I don't know what exactly that nurse thought, what she thought when she kissed me and then she said, "Our doctor is alive." They had probably heard that I was supposed to have been killed. I don't know what personally she thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But yesterday didn't you say that Sarajevo television had announced that you were dead?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did the nurse that you saw really believe that you were dead?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. That's a very speculative question as to what is going on in the person's mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the witness has already explained he didn't know what she thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The point is, sir, the stories people tell sometimes, they turn out not to be true; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I object to that. Again, it is not directed to the evidential point or appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you about -- I believe you testified it was the 19th of April when someone from the HVO military police picked you up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the person's name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Calic. He was a military policeman, he wore white cross-belts, and he used to be a member of the Territorial Defence, and I knew him somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you feel, at the time that he picked you up, that you were being forced to go to the health centre, or was his presence there some sort of a protection for you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I indicated that when my mother-in-law asked him why they wanted to see me, he told her that he wanted to see the doctor, that he didn't want to talk to her. But he told me right away, "Doctor, have no fears. I have come to fetch you. You have to do some work for us." And I got ready and I went with him. And I knew the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you would travel to and from work at the health centre, did you receive any kind of military escort?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: From my apartment to the place where I worked, as of the 18th? Yes, there is -- the distance is maybe 500 metres, and each time I would be accompanied by Dragan Petrovic, who was wearing a military uniform, he would escort me all the way to the apartment, that is, to the entrance to my building, and I would be picked up to go to work by car. The residents, civilians from that building, would always be at the entrance to the building with weapons, so I could not leave the building just like that because of the guards at the entrance to the building, and I was advised not to do that. Sometimes I would be picked up early in the morning, but most of the time I spent at my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So with respect to the guards in front of your house, did you view them as people that were protecting you from the violence that was occurring outside, or were they people that were holding you captive somehow?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: My children and all other Muslims were forbidden to leave the building except when they were being evicted, but then they wouldn't come back after that. These people couldn't do anything once the soldiers in uniform were there. They wanted to get hold of the apartment, and they would simply throw people out and move into these apartments. When I left my apartment, after I had left it, some people broke into it during the night, and apparently they were prevented by the civilian police of the Vitez HVO from mistreating my family. My wife told me that a civilian policeman came with his patrol and prevented the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I guess if you could answer the question as I phrased it: Were they people that were protecting you from the violence outside or were they holding you captive?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, really. They were civilians, elderly people who were not of military age. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you completed --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of them were our neighbours, elderly people, civilians, Croats. We used to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have the same question with respect to the people that would take you from your apartment building to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That would appear, Your Honour, to be a compound type of question. He is asking, Which of two options I am giving you were they performing? I think it should be put slightly differently as to what was the purpose of their escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, the witness should be able to explain that according to what he understood the escorts to be for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Later, I asked them, and one of them told me, that they were in charge of protecting the personnel, especially myself. They were supposed to accompany me everywhere, they were supposed to check on my conduct, see the people I was talking to, calling on the telephone. They were present there all the time. One of them was their chief, and his name was Dragan Petrovic, also known as Kinez. He used to drive me from my workplace to my apartment, and later, when I went to Busovaca, a driver from Busovaca would come to fetch me, and he would drive me to work and back home to my apartment in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand now that you've described what you were doing, but I'm asking you for your own personal feeling. These things that they were doing, accompanying you, et cetera, did that make you feel more secure or were you under some sort of captivity, that you were taken and forced to work at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: These people who drove me were very fair to me, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I would like to use Prosecution Exhibit 1, if available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It should be available. Mr. Misetic, do you want him to use the board or the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The ELMO would be fine with me. I don't know whether it is convenient, though, for the registrar. Yes, that would be great. That's what I was anticipating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you see -- are we ready? You see Vitez on the map there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness use the pointer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the court, please, when the conflict with the Serbs first started?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, generally, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it started with the attack on the village of Ravne, then Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just the time, month and year.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the war in Bosnia started in the first half of 1992. I don't know exactly in which month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At some point, sir, was there armed conflict with the Serbs on this territory that we're looking at on the map, or perhaps in the Travnik-Jajce area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Those are Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you mean in Vitez itself, in the municipality of Vitez? Are you referring to the area of Vitez alone? Counsel, are you referring to the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Vitez and Travnik. I know Travnik, I don't believe, is on that map, but if you could show the court where Travnik is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Travnik would be here, in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there a front-line in that direction that you've just indicated with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it was located on Vlasic mountain, and it was in the immediate vicinity of Travnik, maybe some 12 kilometres, in the village of Turbe, but you can't see Turbe on this map here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you a question here: The map does show what appears to be a road from -- I don't know whether Novi Travnik is on the map -- through Vitez and down to Busovaca. Was that road used as a communication on the front-line against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The road to Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: You can't see Novi Travnik here. It's in this direction, but it's not on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. But the road from Busovaca to Vitez, do you see that main road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This is Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, from Vitez to the north-west, the road appears to extend?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then farther -- no, north-west.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was that road used as a communication and a resupply on the front-line up north-west where the Serb line was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in this region, how long the conflict -- I should say, when the conflict with the Serbs began in that north-west area and when it ended?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think that the first conflict with the BiH army -- with the former JNA took place in 1992. We, at the crisis staff, adopted a decision, we thought that it was not desirable at the time for convoys from Croatia and Slovenia with military equipment use this particular road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Whose convoy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The former Yugoslav People's Army. This was in the first half of 1992. These convoys would be stopped. They were prevented from passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When did this conflict on this territory with the JNA or the Serbs end?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The first conflict took place on the 4th of May when Territorial Defence units, together with HVO units, attacked the base in Travnik. This took place at the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, I mean, the end of the conflict. Was that at the signing of the Dayton accords?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict of the BH army with the army of what is now known as the Armija Republika Srpska ended with the Dayton agreement, and the conflict of the BH army and the HVO ended with the signing of the Washington agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On this map now, could you show the court where Serb lines were? I'm sorry. In the Vitez municipality, were there Serb lines anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, outside the Vitez municipality but still on this map, were there any Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Turbe and Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Anywhere around Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not very familiar with that particular area, but I believe that the front-lines were further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have one more line of questioning. I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can continue. We are breaking off at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what kind of car did you have in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I had a Opel, Opel Kadett.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that the car that was stolen by the HVO military police that you testified to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which car was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: One day I gave my car to a colleague of mine, I lent it to him, and he had a traffic accident with my car, and since I needed a car, I took my brother's car, a Golf, because I had to have a car because of my work. So what was taken from my garage was the car belonging to my brother but which I drove at the time and which my brother lent me because of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought it was your official car, that it was a car that was given to you as a part of your function as the head of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the time head of the medical centre in October and in November 1992, and during that period, I had an official vehicle, a Yugo, and one day, the military police of the HVO requisitioned that car from me in front of the town hall. After that, another director of the medical centre was appointed, it was a Croat by the name of Zvonko Kajic, and maybe ten or fifteen days later, I was replaced by another director.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you had a Yugo taken from you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: My car was stolen, that is the car that belonged to my brother but which I was using at the time. But when I was in Vitez, when I was head of the medical centre, the HVO military police requisitioned my official car, the Yugo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you -- again, I'd like to use the ELMO for this. I'm going to show you a copy of your testimony in the Blaskic case. Do you recall testifying in that case, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, do you think we can finish cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have a few more questions for him, about 10 to 20 questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm referring in the record of the case of the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic, testimony of Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic on the 20th of August, 1997, at pages 1658 and 1659. Sorry, 1659. I apologise. 1659 and 1660. I cite you to line 15, Doctor: "Just to give you an example, temporarily I was director of the Dom Zdravlja in Vitez because my predecessor had left this, Dr. Dzevald Balta. He did this by way of demonstration because he said he had no conditions to work properly. In the Dom Zdravlja, it is the worker's council who appoint the director. I was asked to take over this post before a new director was elected. I used an official car." Move it up, please. Is that the end of the page? "One day" -- all the way up, please. "One day, the military police of the HVO simply came" -- don't zoom in, please. "One day, the military police of the HVO simply came in and said, 'Hello doctor', and I said hello. 'We have been ordered to take away the keys of your car.'" Next page, please. "That is an example. Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, the acting director of the Dom Zdravlja in Vitez, had his car keys to his official car taken over from the HVO military police ..." And then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stated that Dr. Dzevald Balta, was an official director of the health centre in Vitez, that is Dom Zdravlja, and I also stated that he had given up his position, he took some time off, vacation. He said that he could no longer work there because of the conditions, working conditions there. And the workers council asked me to take over this function because Dr. Dzevald Balta left one person behind to replace him, a person by the name of Dragan. At that time, I was an acting director of the health centre; and in front of the municipal hall where I had been to see Marijan Skopljak, the Minister of Defence, because I needed his help with something because the official medical officer of the HVO told me that there was a training of the HVO soldiers in camps, and apparently some skin diseases had spread and lice. So I was looking for Dr. Bruno Buzuk, who was in charge of that, but I didn't find him, I found Marijan Skopljak, whom I knew very well. So I told him the reason why I was there, and since I was in charge of medical protection at the crisis staff, I knew that they had a reserve of necessary medication. My friend, Franjo Tibold, is an epidemiologist, and when I got out of the building, military police approached me and they told me, "We were to take possession of your keys. It's an official order." So I went back -- I went to my office and I called Marijan Skopljak, who was acting Minister of Defence of the HVO for the municipality of Vitez, and I asked him the reason why my vehicle had been requisitioned, and he promised that he would take care of that, but nothing happened. Some ten or fifteen days later, Zvonko Kajic was appointed director of the medical centre in Vitez. This is what I stated. This was my testimony. I apologise for being perhaps too broad, but this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Shall we take a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take a lunch break, and this afternoon, for today only, we shall resume at 14.15, quarter past two this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will continue with the cross-examination, Mr. Misetic, in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, first just as a preliminary matter I would like to ask you, have you discussed your testimony during the lunch break with anyone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, the time was very short. I hardly had any lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I could take you back for a moment and add to some testimony or some questioning that we did a little bit earlier. I would ask you to use the pseudonym "Witness A" in any response you give. You referred the person, Witness A, to your colleague; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I asked her to take her and try to treat her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you subsequent to that get any type of report from your colleague after an examination was performed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had other responsibilities. And with my colleague, I talked and she told me that she had many women undergoing treatment at the time. She didn't tell me how many. She simply told me that she was working with women like Witness A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you received no specific information about Witness A?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, now I'd like to follow up where we left off at the lunch break. Again, a couple of questions about the car. Just so I'm clear. . Your official car was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And your personal car was involved in a car accident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was earlier when my own car suffered and I had lent it to my friend, Dragan Sefradin, and he was in an accident so that my car was broken, and I had it repaired. It was a car mechanic Franjic in -- I can't remember exactly what his name was. So my own car was being repaired, my personal car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then the car that you had borrowed from your brother was also taken from you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, what is the point about the car?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He identifies Mr. Furundzija yesterday in his direct testimony with respect to trying to take his car, and I'm getting to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I beg to correct my friend there. I think the conversation he alluded to with Mr. Furundzija was that Furundzija asked for the car keys, said he knew where the garage was, et cetera, but I don't think he was demanding his "car" or mentioned any car by name or description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I said he was trying to take his car. I presume when he allegedly tried to take the keys that it was for the purpose of taking the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need go into that now, but I think if we can move on a bit towards the central point, it would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you identified yesterday as the person who tried to take the keys from your car as Mr. Furundzija; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How long did that encounter take?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: A couple of minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that conversation just the one sentence that you said or two sentences, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That was all, what I already said, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So two sentences; perhaps, it was a 30-second encounter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whatever it took, I mean, he did not stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that you had never before met Mr. Furundzija; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I said I did not know him well. I don't say that I did not see him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So where would you see him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that that gentleman was one of the commanders of the military police of the Territorial Defence, and I used to see him, seeing that I was a physician. I saw him in the company of a young man who was an active military officer, Zikret Ahmic. I saw them patrolling together on a couple of times, and I saw him in various places, but I never talked to him. I asked the commander, "How could he be the commander of the military police?" And he told me, "Well, he's a good bloke." Who was it? I think Hakija Cengic, and the other one I also knew, Zlatko, and he told me -- we also have a Zlatko who is with the military police. That is where I saw him. I can't remember seeing him before, although I know some of his relatives. Personally, I did not know him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After you went to Zenica, did you see any pictures of Anto Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So your identification of Mr. Furundzija is based on your memory from --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose I can state it before the court that I saw him on television. On television, I saw when the accused Croats were being sent away, and that was the news, so I saw it on the Croatian television, however, them being seen off, but no other pictures, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you saw Mr. Furundzija in October of '97 when the group of ten Bosnian Croats voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: On television, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And on television, you were able to identify Mr. Furundzija; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was a news agency news and I saw so many men. No, no, I was watching -- no, it wasn't then. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me move on. Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I should ask the court first, for leave of the Trial Chamber, since identification is going to be in issue in this case, if we could have Mr. Furundzija with an escort stand here and we can do a height, weight, et cetera, and ask the witness whether he is in the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Furundzija the same height as you recall him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I used to see Mr. Furundzija in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Height?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really confirm it, whether he has grown up or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said he came and took you out of the health centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you identified him yesterday in court; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question again for the reporter was "And you identified him yesterday in court?" You are a medical doctor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You're used to taking people's height, weight?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The nurses do that. I don't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you look at the information and you use that information in healing patients; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I use it when I need it, only when I need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question to you then, again, Doctor is: Is Mr. Furundzija approximately the same height as he was when you say you saw him in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. I came out for a couple of minutes. It was an encounter, and I told you that when I came out, he told me what he told me and that was that. I never paid any attention. And since I -- I mean, when I worked, I was constantly under the pressure of fear. In Vitez, I knew that I was, what, the president of the war presidency, and I had heard that very many of my associates had been killed. I expected that I would be killed. And I don't know if you can understand it, I'm a doctor, but I was under a constant pressure. I was very tense. And you are asking me something that, at that particular moment, I simply paid no attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you pay attention to his weight?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a soldier, Anto Furundzija, before me whom I knew as a military policeman of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question is, Doctor: Is he approximately the same weight as he was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I cannot confirm it or not. I just can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you, Doctor, about his hair. Is his hair the same length as it was at the time you saw him in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I told you that he was wearing a combat uniform, so I could not see his hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did he have his uniform on his head, Doctor? He had his uniform on his head?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He had a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I do protest the tone of that particular question. By "uniform," would he ask specifically what kind of thing he's suggesting? I mean, just saying "his uniform on his head" seems somewhat of an inappropriate way to put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness has answered he had a cap.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He had a cap, a military cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What kind of cap was it? Describe the cap.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: A camouflage -- the kind of camouflage head gear, military one, with this thing with the shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did he have any other identification as to which army he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that I had paid no attention to that. Only HVO soldiers came for treatment there, by and large. And when somebody pulls you away from your work, and I was shocked by the question, and I simply paid no attention to markings, to insignia or whatever, I really paid no attention to that. I immediately went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the time you met the man who took you out, did you get a good look at his face?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking him in the eye, just as I'm looking now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you can't identify height, weight, hair?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, about the hair, he had a cap, so you can't push that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what he says he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness says he had a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking him: Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We just want to clarify something, sir. I asked you whether you had seen a photograph which you may have misconstrued as, "Have you seen a photograph in Zenica?" Have you ever seen a photograph outside of the television occurrence, or something like that with respect to what you had testified to earlier, have you ever seen any photograph at any time since April of 1993 of Mr. Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw Furundzija's photograph, except on television, but it wasn't until then, it was some agency news, not when they were being seen off, and I don't watch television much. But I heard it on the news that he had been arrested, that Furundzija had been arrested, and I think they mentioned another name too, and they showed their pictures on television. I think he was much heavier. I think he has grown thinner. On television, he looked much heavier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before you came to testify, were you aware that you were going to have to make a courtroom ID of Mr. Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you one more exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the accused sit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the accused can sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First let me ask the question: Sir, you said you worked with Enes Surkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah -- I mean, things that I needed came in the typed form. I did not see his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Our examination is concluded, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you weren't in Nadioci, Bosnia at the location called "the Bungalow" on the 15th of May, 1993, were you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of May, what year? I only passed through in a military ambulance when I was being transported from Vitez to Busovaca and back. When I would finish with my work there, they took me back to Vitez, but I paid no attention to bungalows. Once, they took me in the military ambulance through the village of Ahmici so I could see what it looked like, but personally I did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, Your Honours, but I would at this stage --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no re-examination at this stage. What I would like to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I've failed to move into evidence the few exhibits that I did want to move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I was going to ask for the same thing for the Prosecution, Madam President, so would it be possible for us, perhaps, jointly to move that we move the exhibits for the Prosecution and the Defence into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, all four? There are five or four?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there are six and, no, we only want to move in Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Exhibit 3, which is the witness's statement, but only with respect to page 8 of the statement, the last four sentences of the first long paragraph on that page, and page 10, of course, which is his acknowledgement that he signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would suggest that it be more proper that the document as a whole should be entered into evidence, because a document is a whole, and to say a selective quotation could be misleading at the end of the day when reviewing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic, the whole statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've only asked him with respect to that small portion of the statement. The rest of it he has been examined on by the Prosecution and the Defence. There's no need to move in the entire statement. We asked him with respect to that specific portion and whether his witness acknowledgement on the last page was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but it can't be taken out of context. It has to be the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the court wants to move that whole paragraph in then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, it's the Defence who have introduced the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the court will allow us then to move the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that paragraph then for contextual purposes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, you would like the whole statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just thought it was more appropriate that if one is referring to any contents of a document, then potentially that entire document becomes admissible as one single exhibit. It's a matter for you to rule, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall admit the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, we withdraw the statement, so we will only move in Exhibit 1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So D-3, D-4 and D-2 should be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: D-2, we would move it in if the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, you only need D-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: D-1, right, but there was a question as to authenticity before. If the Prosecution still has that question, fine; otherwise, we'd move it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, do you mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, my query as regards Exhibit D-2, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, D-1, you have no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: D-1, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. D-2?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, D-2 was a document where there could not, from the evidence that I heard from the witness, there could be no authentication. It wasn't a list produced by him. He simply confirmed his name as a candidate or something, so not even that he was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was only asking counsel if they had an objection. If they do --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- we will leave it out. D-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So D-1, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just in regards to the Prosecution exhibits, just 1 and 2, Ma'am, the two maps, perhaps if you would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the two maps were already entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What number, Registrar? The documents for identification only will be returned to the registrar. Thank you very much, Doctor, for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I interpose for a moment? I would like you to consider the formality of releasing the witness. I don't know if my friends for the Defence have any problem or objection to him being released so that he can return home. This impacts on what the Victim and Witness Unit would be able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, we will not be recalling the witness. He may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I so apply then, Madam. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving evidence at the Tribunal. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, ladies and gentlemen of the Prosecution and gentlemen of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask that prior to the next witness coming in that the protective measures that the court has ordered be in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is witness ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This is Witness B, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution -- is that the pseudonym and voice distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, those are the protections that have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The face distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Face distortion and the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, do we have the English translation of the statement of Witness B?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that that has been given to the court. If you would like another copy, we can certainly provide it

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness make the solemn declaration whilst standing, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth WITNESS B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I begin, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness B. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you ready to begin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few background questions first. Witness B, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is Ahmici located in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you lived in Ahmici all of your life?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you went to school in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber a bit about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school and also secondary school. I was trained as a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell the Tribunal, did you live in Ahmici in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you live with your family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please describe the house that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was our family house. It was a two-storey house with a yard and some attachments to it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the house have a basement to it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the house near a main road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the court in which directions did the road lead?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was the main road which connected Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Turning your attention now to the morning of April 16th, 1993. Might I ask you, were you at home?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was your family with you that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: My mother was with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please take your time and describe for the Chamber what, if anything, happened to you and your mother that morning on April 16th.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was early in the morning and I woke up to the sounds of shooting and explosions. I got up, and at that moment, an incendiary bullet entered our room, our living room, which was on the first floor of the house. It fell on a couch, which caught fire. I took some water and put it out, but I panicked and I didn't know what to do at the time, so I went to the telephone, I wanted to call my relatives, I wanted to find out what was happening, but the lines were cut off. Then I went to my mother and I told her that that part of the house was not safe. The shooting was going on all the time, and the house could easily catch fire. So I told my mother that we should go downstairs to the lower part of the house, that is, to the basement, and that we would be safer there. So my mother and I went downstairs to the basement, but in the front of the house, there were three soldiers in uniform --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I stop you just for a moment there? Now, you mentioned that there were three soldiers in uniform. Could you please tell us where they were coming from, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: They had come from the lower part of the village, from the lower part of the house, from the direction of the main road, and two of them came from the upper part. They were also wearing uniform. And they pushed us with their hands, my mother and myself, into the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you say that two came from the upper house and three came from below the house, do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection. She did not -- that is not the testimony. She said there were three total.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, I am trying to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then I object to it as leading the witness. The witness has testified as three and the question is posed as two came from one and three from the other. I think that is highly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have clarification then from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many soldiers were present who came to your house in this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection again. Asked and answered. She said three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That was not the question that was asked, and I would like to have it clarified as the Judge has requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question was: "Now, you mentioned that there were three soldiers in uniform. Could you please tell us where they were coming from, if anywhere?" Now you're asking again how many soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have this clarified by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's been verified. She doesn't like the answer to the question, and now it's being reposed, and it's already been told to the witness what she's looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
