utterances.text: All right. The Trial Chamber would like clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness B, would you please tell us how many soldiers were at the house that day during that incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There were five of them in total, but you haven't listened to me to the end. There were two groups of soldiers. Three came from below the house and two came from above -- from the area above the house. That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then could you please describe what occurred after that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: They pushed us into the basement, they pushed my mother and myself, and they entered as well. Then they started cursing, "Our balijas mother," they were saying, "What are you doing? This is all doing of your Alija." They abused us verbally, and one of the soldiers told me that I should go and call our neighbours, and he wanted to know where the men were. At that moment, I turned around and started talking to one of the soldiers whom I knew, and I asked him, "Anto, could I put my shoes on and take my jacket" because I didn't know whether there was anyone in these houses. I had just got up. And I told him, "You know me very well. You know I've never been a nationalist." I had lots of friends. I had friends among Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I could ask right now, when you're referring to "Anton," could you please tell me how Anton was dressed, this person you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was he armed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please now continue with the conversation that you were having with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He kept quiet, he didn't say anything in response to that, and the other soldiers were searching the house, throwing things about the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this person that you referred to as "Anton," is this someone that you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did you know the person from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him from school. We used to go to school together for four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Had you seen him after that time period in which you attended school together?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We used to see each other later, after school, in town and in cafes. I used to see him. He was a member of the Territorial Defence, and I would often see him in a car in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Witness B, I would like you to look very carefully around the courtroom today and tell me if you see the person that you are referring to in your testimony as "Anton"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please describe for me what the person is wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He's wearing a black blazer, white shirt, and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please point to him for me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would the record reflect that Witness B has pointed to the accused, Anton Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the accused has been identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness B, might I ask you: Does Anton Furundzija look the same today as he did that morning in your basement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He's a bit heavier today, I think, and he's dressed differently, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you: What were the other soldiers doing in your basement while you were having a conversation with Anto Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Other soldiers were searching the house, throwing things around. They were looking for something, I don't know what they were looking for, but they were searching the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did they find anything in this search of your house?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honours, as to the relevance of this line of questioning. The events on 16 April, '93, have no relevance outside of the identification. I don't understand what some other soldiers' conduct has to do with whether Mr. Furundzija was present on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But that question is -- there is nothing wrong with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure, there is. It has no relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What do you mean? The witness has just started describing what happened to her and her family when the soldiers, in which group the accused was, arrived at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, we would object as to -- I don't know what that has to do with the issues in this case but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I repeat the question: Did the soldiers find anything in your house that morning, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then could you please tell me, when you were having your conversation with Anto Furundzija, about how close were you standing to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was maybe one metre away from him. I was really standing next to him. It was a small room, and we were standing close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, standing at that closeness to him, could you see whether there was a patch on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: "Jokers" on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then could you please describe for the Trial Chamber how you and your mother left the basement that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: They pushed us out, they told us that we could not stay there. They said they had to leave -- that we had to leave, and they mentioned "Our Alija" again. So we left the basement, we got out of the basement, but my mother wouldn't leave the house. She wanted to stay there. So she turned around; she wanted to go back. And at that moment, one of the soldiers shot at our feet, so the earth covered our feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness B, did the earth cover your feet due to the gunshots that were fired?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you also please tell the Trial Chamber what else was happening in Ahmici from your vantage point that morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm going to have to make an objection as to what relevance what else was going on in Ahmici has to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Armed conflict, the issue of armed conflict, which you said you are not conceding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us any other things you saw going on in Ahmici that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That morning in Ahmici, the houses were on fire, there was a lot of smoke. We could smell the smoke, smell of gunfire. We heard shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there other families that were --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Smell of gun powder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me. Were there other families that were standing outside of their houses also that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, that is when we were told to leave the house, one of the soldiers motioned with his hand to Ismail Ahmic with his wife and to Mujo Ahmic, who was also there with his wife and his two children. So they came to my house. At that moment, we women were told to leave, to run away, and Mujo and Ismail Ahmic remained there on that spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Mujo and Ismail Ahmic since that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did they remain with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did the group of women go at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We reached the main road, and I managed to cast a glance from that point, and I saw from the main road, I saw one of the soldiers spilling something from a jerrycan on my house and one part of the house was already on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you then leave Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We set off in the direction of Pirici, but shooting was going on all the time. We had no specific place we wanted to go; we didn't know where to go. We passed the house of the woman by the name of Mejra. That house was not on fire, had not been set on fire, and Mejra called us, she motioned to us, and she invited us into her house because of the shooting, and we had to take shelter somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So how long did you stay in Mejra's house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed in Mejra's house until the evening of the 16th, until dusk. Her neighbour arrived at that point, a Croat woman, and she told us that we were not safe there. So she took us to the house of her daughter, where we spent the night, the night between the 16th and the 17th, we stayed at that house. On the following morning, the morning of the 17th, my mother simply couldn't believe that our house had been burned down and she went to the house. She wanted to get something, some documents, some of our belongings because we hadn't taken anything from our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I stop you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: So she left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you referring that your mother went back to the house in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She went back to the house on the 17th -- in the morning of the 17th of April. So when she came back from the house, she was very frightened, she seemed lost, and I asked her what had happened, and then she told me that the house had been completely burned down. She had seen dead bodies in the vicinity of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did the group go that morning when your mother returned from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When she returned, another Croat woman whom I didn't know arrived, and she told this other woman that we were supposed to move to another house where there was a shop and that we were all supposed to be collected there and then that they would see what to do with us. But anyhow, we were supposed to gather there in the shop. So we went to that house. We passed Mejra's house on the way to the shop, and that house too was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that the house that you had stayed in the previous day as you were fleeing Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed in that house, yes, and it was not damaged while we were there on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you had gone to a shop with the group. Could you please describe for the Trial Chamber what occurred when you were in the shop?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This shop consisted of one room, and there were lots of women and children in that shop. Each woman had suffered personal tragedy, losing husbands, sons. There were a couple of men as well. But when we got in, when we entered that shop, a group of soldiers wearing black uniforms arrived, and they started searching for men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did they eventually take these men away?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They took away Hasim Ahmic. His wife protested. He begged them not to take him away. He was an elderly man, quite ill, and they simply told us to keep quiet or else we would all be killed. Then they also took out Munib Helub (phoen), Amir Ramic and Zenur Ramic, two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether their families have seen those men since that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, they haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness B, then on the morning of April 18th, did the remaining women move to a different location?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were moved to the building of Dubravica Elementary School.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived there on foot, and Nikica Plavcic was the one who escorted us. There was one red van that also accompanied that group. It was a group of women consisting of maybe a hundred, maybe even more women.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How long did it take you to arrive at the school that morning by foot?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe half an hour, one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you arrived there, could you tell me how many people were in the school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in the school, we were met there by a group of soldiers who separated us. Some younger women and children were taken to one room, and the remaining women were taken to the gym. There were several men in that gym, they had been there already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the people who were detained in that school, Witness B, were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were residents of Novaci, Rijeka, and other neighbouring villages in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The soldiers who were around the school, could you please tell me what nationality they were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were wearing HVO insignia. Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like you now to tell the Trial Chamber a bit of the conditions that existed at the school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: "Conditions"? You can hardly call them "conditions." It was a gym and there was nothing in there, so they brought some mattresses, and I think that maybe five or six women slept on one mattress. We didn't get any food for about two or three days. Almost every day, a group of soldiers would come and take men for digging, and we lived in a constant fear all the time. We could hear that the -- we could hear Croat soldiers shooting because each time we would hear gunfire. We were simply human shields at that time and in that location. There were days that we were not allowed to get up to leave the place at all. There was only one toilet in the building used by everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How many days did you stay at this school with your mother?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Twelve days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you eventually leave the school around May 1st?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of May, we left the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you return to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no possibility for us to return to Ahmici. We were registered by these Croatian soldiers, and they told us that we had only two options: Zenica or Travnik. Nobody even bothered to ask us to stay there, whether we wanted to stay. So on the 1st of May, I left for Zenica with my mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber a bit about your life during the month of May after you left the school?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Terrible. We had nothing, no clothes. A refugee belonging nowhere, having nothing. I simply was left without anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness B, for you, did the war start on the morning of April 16th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness B, I know this is difficult for you, so we appreciate you coming to The Hague, and I'm going to try to keep my questions short so you can leave quicker. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: (Nods)

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th, you stated that you and your mother were in the house. Was anyone else in the house with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was your father in Vranjska at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He left a day before, for a day to help my aunt. I think they had to saw some timber or something. So that he wasn't there even a day before, they did not finish the job, and he did not return that evening. And for three months, he knew nothing about our lot, nor did we know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have your 1995 statement, and I want to show you a small passage there and ask you just a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement you gave to the Tribunal, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This is in English. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would note to the court that we never got a signed copy of the statement. I don't know if the Prosecutor wants to stipulate that it's the statement or produce a signed copy, if they have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are you talking about the statement -- there is a page with witness acknowledgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't think -- mine is not signed, anyway. I don't know whether the court has a Bosnian version that is signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no. We have the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I was looking at the last page. You're right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 4, ma'am. Do you see the witness acknowledgement? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 2? It's approximately halfway down. For the court, the witness doesn't speak English. I will try to read it. It is the last underlined --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would just like to note for the record, again, the fact that Defence counsel is acting as our interpreter should just be noted, as opposed to having an official translation, if you would like to refer that part of the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have the same comment as I did this morning. I didn't have time during the lunch break to have the statement translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This statement was not provided to the court in the original language, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It does not exist in the original language, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's okay if the Defence counsel reads it in English and then the official interpretation is done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that that would be more proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant. I wasn't going to do it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. So whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the court will note that there's an underlined sentence, at least on the copy I provided, and the sentence right after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The sentence reads: "When Anto asked me to go to the home of Dzidic and see where the men were. I said I cannot do this. It is impossible."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that statement, Ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I said, that perhaps it was because of the translation or something, but one of the soldiers told me to go there and asked me if there were any men there, and then I turned to Anto because I was at a loss of what to do. They were trying to force me to go and then I turned to Anto and I said I just got up. I don't know whether anyone is there. May I put some shoes on or take a jacket?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I should say you did not do what that soldier asked you to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go. I put the shoes on but I did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you refused to do as you were told, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you struck in any way?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not struck, but they were -- I mean, they fired, as I said, down on the ground in front of my mother's and my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the house when you didn't do what you were asked to do, no one struck you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I hate to ask you this question, but it's important for this case, Ma'am. No one attempted to sexually assault you, did they?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, I think that is completely outside of the scope of the direct of this examination. I think that is a question that is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, what was your reason for objecting? You're saying it was outside of what the examination-in-chief is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. There's been no testimony offered that Mr. Furundzija in any way touched anyone that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber thinks that it's a proper question to ask because this was a confrontation. We may as well hear what other details there could have been. The witness may answer the question. Maybe you can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No one attempted to sexually assault you that day, did they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The same applies to your mother?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You never saw Anto Furundzija order anybody to do that to you, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes that the witness said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please speak up so that the interpreters can pick up your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The answer, can you repeat the answer to the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase the question so it's cleaner in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You never saw Anto Furundzija order anybody to do that to you, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, no, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, who told you to go to the main road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: One of those soldiers, one of the group. You must realise, it was careless. Everything happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is it possible that one of those soldiers was Anto Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know because it was as we were coming out of the house, and other soldiers stayed behind, except for one who was in front of the house and who called to those others to join him, so I don't know. I'm not sure. I can't say something that I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't exclude the possibility, then, that Anto Furundzija is the one that told you to go to the main road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I just don't know. I told you and in my statement too, that Anto never talked to me. I did talk to him but he kept silent all the while and just stood there. He simply did not talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You ultimately followed the advise you received and went down to the main road by the Pican Kafana (phoen); correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We simply couldn't do anything else. I told you that they fired in front of our feet. It's not that we were obedient. We simply had no other choice. I mean, when somebody fires in front of your feet, is it that you obedience or is it that you do it simply because you must.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness B, did Anto Furundzija come to your house among five soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honours, I think that has been covered in direct examination. Has it not been covered in direct examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: She simply wants it emphasised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, Mr. Misetic, it's not in dispute is it, that he was there? Are you disputing that he was there that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter of commenting. I'm asking you to tell us what your case is. Is it disputed that the accused was there the day that the witness said he was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not a witness, but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. Misetic. What is your case about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My case is, Your Honours, regardless of what happened on that day, it has no relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be, but the evidence has now been given that he was there. If you're disputing that he was there, then you must put it to the witness so that she can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I never disputed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, so we take it that the matter is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can't speak for the court. I'm just saying that there was an objection as to starting to go over the same testimony that was elicited on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I now know that it's much more important that the Prosecution goes through it because, although you are not disputing it entirely, you weren't saying in terms that it's not in dispute. Therefore the Prosecution are perfectly entitled to ask the question. I would allow it. Would you ask the question again, Ms. Sellers, and make it quite plain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was Anto Furundzija with the group of soldiers that came to your house on the morning of April 16th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were the group of soldiers armed and in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: They pushed you in the house and did they search your house after that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And eventually was it among the men in that group of soldiers that ordered you and your mother to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, are you certain that the Anto Furundzija with whom you are referring to on that day is the Anto Furundzija who is sitting in court today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I have an opportunity to ask two or three questions, since it's been re-opened on redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I would just like to ask, I don't know if there is the opportunity to re-re-cross within the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, but she was simply repeating what was in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In lieu of Judge May's comments and in lieu of the fact that she has repeated the direct examination, verbatim, practically, I would like the opportunity to raise just a couple of issues since it is now in issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will limit it to three questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I believe that he had that opportunity on cross. If he feels it was the nexus of my direct examination, that is the basis and that was the scope of his cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And she had the opportunity in direct and then she repeated her direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: One of the purposes of re-examination is to clear up what was raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Exactly. I would like to clear something up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think that would be proper, Mr. Misetic, sorry. Any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's exactly what I was going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you have the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, might the Prosecution ask to take a small break prior to bringing in the other witness. We would like to check something with the Victim and Witness Unit about the other witnesses and be able to inform the court of their status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we rise, the Trial Chamber would like to find out from the Defence how much time they think they will need for the Defence case. Just an estimate, because we have two other cases ongoing, so we would like to know whether we will need to reschedule this case, if we can't finish it next week, because we are continuing next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would need some more time beyond next week, due to scheduling difficulties with one of the witnesses. I would rather not discuss it at the moment. I would discuss it in camera, ex parte, if the court wants to know, but our cases, I would imagine, wouldn't take any longer than three days, and I would also throw in the caveat that much of it depends on what is elicited from the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it your position that you would be able, perhaps, after the next witness, at least we have gone halfway, after the next witness, for instance, we shall have gone halfway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe I can raise that again in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As you heard in my opening statement, the only real witnesses from our position, the only real witness is Witness A and so it depends on what happens with Witness A, regardless of what happens with the halfway point witness. I will again tell the court that at this time we plan no more than three days for our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the other cases that are scheduled, we wouldn't be able to have even a week before October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't be able to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Even a week before October, so we wanted you to have this in mind so that by the end, maybe, of this week, you can be able to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we don't complete it by the end of next week, we have to wait until October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Most likely because the other cases are ongoing, and there is a problem of the courtroom. When we think about it, we will re-open it at another stage before the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The court will rise and we may raise this issue before we rise finally today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How many minutes did you say you wanted? Maybe we will just take our normal break, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness make the solemn declaration standing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Witness C for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Protective measures, face distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Face distortion and the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Pseudonym, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. WITNESS C

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you ready to begin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness C, would you please tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that Vitez which is in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you lived in Vitez most of your adult life?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I grew up there and I lived there as an adult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please inform the Trial Chamber of your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Bosnian and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Might I turn your attention now to April 16th, 1993. Were you living in Vitez on that date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I lived in Vitez at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen on the morning of April 16th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Because I worked, I had to get up rather early. And on that morning, I got up around five a.m. and I pulled up my blinds and I was surprised to see two houses on fire. My windows were facing old Vitez, so I called my husband and I told him that there was fire. And I looked through the window and I saw some soldiers moving around quickly, so I discussed this with my husband. And as we were talking, we heard a very loud detonation. And then my husband and I, we wrapped our children in blankets, my daughters at that time were aged four and ten, and we hurried downstairs to the basement. Our neighbours were also going downstairs. They all went to the basement and we stood there and waited. The shooting started in the meantime around the building, but we didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did there come a time period then afterwards where you left the basement and you went back up to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Since the children were still in their pyjamas, I had to go back, I had to bring some warm clothes for them. And I looked through the window and I saw another two or three houses on fire in Stari Vitez. So when I came back to the basement, I told my husband, "Something is going wrong. Houses in Stari Vitez are on fire." And the building that was in front of my house that I could see from the window, there were lots of soldiers around that building. And in that building, standing on the window, I could see them better than I saw them in the morning. They were all wearing black uniforms or some of them were wearing camouflage uniforms, but most of them were in black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you see whether the soldiers were armed or not, Witness C?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Though I could see them, I don't remember now. I'm sorry, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you then go back down to the basement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I remained in the basement together with other people who lived in that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did any of the soldiers ever enter into the basement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The entrance to our building was locked, and the tenants had made an agreement amongst themselves that we should not unlock the entrance door because we didn't know what was happening, and this is what we decided. But then we heard a very loud banging on the door and windows being smashed. Then one of my neighbours, she went to the door and she opened the entrance door to the building. Soldiers entered the building. They went upstairs towards the apartments, and some of them went downstairs to the basement. There were quite a few soldiers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then when they went into the basement, could you please tell the court whether they called the Muslim families out or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they said that all Muslims should leave the basement, should get out. They first wanted us to identify ourselves, to show them our ID's, but not everyone had an ID with them, so they told us to go back to our apartments to get the identification papers. And then when quite a few people went upstairs to get these, then they said, "No, only Muslims should leave the basement and only Muslims should come in front of the building."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the soldiers also at that time send people to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they first took us in front of the building, all of us, and they told us to stand in line, men, women. And they had some kind of masks on their faces, stockings that were pulled on their faces, and they stood in front of us with their weapons pointed at us. And I thought this was like an execution squad, and we were crying, and then they told us to keep quiet, that we would all be killed, and there were lots of curses, threats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Witness C, did they send any of the people that were gathered outside of the apartment to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they all went to the cinema, except for myself and another woman who had a very small child. Her child was crying more than others and was hysterical, so the soldiers told her to keep the child quiet, but she didn't manage to do that, so she went back. And because I had a young child as well, they took me back as well. As for my husband and other men, they were all taken to the cinema which was part of the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were the people who went to the cinema Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that your husband was taken to the cinema. Could you tell us how long he stayed there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: He stayed at the cinema until the 30th of April, that is, from the 16th until the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever go to see him in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When they took them there, at first I didn't know that they were there, at the cinema. I didn't know whether they were alive or not. But on the evening of that date, women and children were returned, so they told us that they had all been locked up in the boiler room that was part of the Workers' University, all men. So we kept inquiring but we didn't have any information at the time as to what was happening with them. So we asked whether we could go there and see them, and then one of our neighbours asked the policeman, whether they were soldiers or policemen, I don't really know, but they were all wearing uniform, and he asked them to enable one of the women to go and visit there. So they let me go there and I took some basic things, some food and clothes, and I went to visit my husband for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw when you went to the cinema to visit your husband?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they all looked very exhausted and they were afraid for their children. They were all very dirty. The theatre had a number of seats, but there were too many people in there, so some of them were simply lying down on the floor or sitting down on the floor. All they wanted to know was whether we were alive, whether the children were okay and, you know, how things were in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: While your husband was detained at the cinema, where did you continue to live?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the basement. I spent nine days, nine nights in the basement. I was there all the time. After that, we were allowed to go back to our apartments, but I and a few other neighbours couldn't go back to our apartments because our windows were facing Stari Vitez, so we had to go back to the apartments belonging to other Muslims and the apartments with windows facing the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were still in the basement that you heard another big explosion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened on the third day of our stay in the basement, third day after the war had started in Vitez, the attack in Vitez. Women were probably watching TV at the time because people had brought TV sets in the basement, and we could only watch TV Vitez, which was broadcast by Croats, so I heard stories -- I heard that something was going on. One of our neighbours who was not there at the time, who had gone to Kolonija neighbourhood, she called us and she told me and one of my other neighbours to call her back. So my neighbour called her, and then she told me that this woman had told us to go back to our apartments, to go to her apartment as well, and to open all the windows and that we should not leave the basement after that, that we should not risk our lives because something terrible is going on, something terrible was about to happen. Maybe two or three hours after that, I don't know exactly how long, I went back to get some food for the children. We were able to cook some food in the basement, but we kept the food upstairs in the apartment because we couldn't keep any food in the basement. So when I got -- when I entered the corridor of my apartment, I heard a very loud explosion and I was all covered in dust, and I was thrown away from the corridor and into the stairway. So I quickly ran down to my children. I didn't know at the time what -- I thought that the building would collapse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were staying in the basement again with your children during this time period, was the building guarded by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know what types of soldiers there were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Many soldiers kept coming in and out. There was one soldier who was always there during the night, together with one of the tenants. They kept watch in the building, and we could not leave the basement. I myself didn't pay much attention. I took care of the children. But that part of the basement had been previously used for storing firewood, and this is where we stayed. From one part of the basement, you could see the stairway of the building. It was not a closed-in stairway, it was open. So my children were -- you know how children are -- there were lots of children aged about 12 or 13, and they would make, you know, comments like "Jokers" or "Vitezovi are passing by," this is what I heard from them. I heard children mentioning these names. And I knew that they were Croat soldiers because they had insignia similar to the ones that you would -- to the sign you would see on a flag. But they were all HVO soldiers. And very often they had masks on their faces when they were in the basement or on the stairway, masks with only holes for their eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there any sniping that took place in your building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: While we were in the basement and at the beginning of that period, we were not allowed to go back to our apartments. At one point, they were -- we were ordered not to leave the area, not to go to the stairway. But we heard shooting, we heard shots; and then later on, we would be told not to go to the stairway. But some people managed to go upstairs to their apartments, to the third floor or the fourth floor, and then maybe for -- they would stay there for one hour, half an hour. But shots would be fired from the building and then we would hear more shooting around the building, and it was very -- it was terrible when they would come to the building and when they would shoot from the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain why they would shoot from your building, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I assume -- I mean, I know that they tried to shoot from my apartment because once, when I went back to the apartment, I saw that the curtains were torn; and after that, when we went back to our apartments, when everything returned to normal, we realised that there was some damage in the apartment. For example, one of my neighbours, she had an apartment with a very good view of Stari Vitez, and they fired from her apartment. But I was not present when they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you and your family could move back into an apartment. Did your husband join you from the cinema at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Ten days after he had been taken to the cinema, ten days into his stay in the theatre, he was very sick, so they let him out. I was in the basement, but I would go from time to time to somebody else's apartment. And then in the morning, HVO soldiers came again, and they took him away again. When he came back on the 30th of April, we spent several days in somebody else's apartment, and then after that, we were allowed to go back to our apartment. Our apartment was a terrible mess at the time because they broke the door and we couldn't shut the door after that. They kept coming to our apartment searching for something, and it was not only the case of my apartment but the apartments of other Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you just describe very briefly a bit of your life in the building during the month of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult. It was a very difficult period of time. We were only thinking of how we would survive. The conditions were very bad. We didn't have running water in the basement, we didn't have facilities to wash ourselves, wash the children; and later on, when we went back to the apartments, there would be three families living in one apartment because, for example, I couldn't go back to my own apartment. Shortly after that, we were running out of food. But in the end, we were lucky that we managed to survive this whole situation. We couldn't leave the building, we couldn't go out, we didn't have any contact with the outside world. But because I went to see my husband, I somehow managed to learn what the situation was. I learned about what had happened in Ahmici, I knew that there was a war going on, but I couldn't say that I was very well-informed of the situation. I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you feel that your family was in danger during the month of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in danger ever since the 16th of April because we kept hearing about people getting killed. There was a woman in our apartment building that was killed simply because she was a Muslim. There was no other reason for this killing. So there was a number of such incidents, killing incidents, in our apartment blocks. But that was the only one from our entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Had you heard of Muslims being forced to leave their apartments?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: On May 30th, did two people come to your apartment and inquire about it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, two young men came to my apartment. They were unknown to me, I had never seen them before. They asked me to have my apartment exchanged for an apartment in Zenica, and I was taken by surprise because I never thought that I would leave the apartment. This was the apartment where I had been living ever since 1978. So I was surprised. And I asked them why. I thought these people had a very nice apartment. They told me they had a nice apartment, a bigger one, and they said that they would give me their apartment in Zenica for my apartment in Vitez, and I told them that I wouldn't accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then what did you do directly after that, Witness C?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after that, when I came to my apartment, I told my husband, "Now it's our turn," because this had already happened to several of our neighbours. They would be offered something like that, something similar, and then they would disappear. So I told my husband, "It's our turn now. We have to find some solution."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What was your solution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We found an acquaintance, a Croat, who would take us in his car. We didn't ask him where he was taking us, but it was in the direction of Zenica, in the direction of the road to Zenica, and this is how we went to Zenica. We didn't have much time left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you left the apartment that you had been living in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May I ask you, have you returned to Vitez to live now?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: To my apartment? No, no. And I couldn't live in Zenica because I had no place to live there, so now I am living in a village in the municipality of Vitez in somebody else's house together with two other families again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Tribunal the reason that you cannot go back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: They're not allowing us to go back. A Croat family has moved in our apartment in the meantime and they're living there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you say "us," do you mean Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Muslims. They're not allowing Muslims to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination, if any?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about what happened to you after you left the Vitez municipality and you went on to Zenica. When you arrived there, who took care of the refugees such as yourself in the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When I left Vitez, I went to my sister-in-law, my father's sister, who lived in Zenica, she got married there, and she had a two-room apartment, and there were twelve of us living at that apartment at the time. This is the reason why I went back to that village, because I could no longer stay there. It was only later on that I was registered with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the people in Vitez -- or, I should say, the refugees from Vitez that arrived in Zenica, did you communicate often with each other about your experiences in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In particular, there was a school in Zenica where the inhabitants of Ahmici, who became refugees in Zenica, were housed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You would go there and hear the stories that the people from Ahmici were telling about what happened to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I heard stories from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did everyone from Vitez eventually talk to these people and hear the stories coming out of Vitez, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I would ask that the question be narrower. The witness would have no knowledge if everyone from Vitez heard these stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it, if she likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All of the people from Vitez that you had contact with, did they come to eventually hear the story of what happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were there stories about who was involved in that attack?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Croats attacked Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At some point were you asked by the authorities in Zenica to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever given another statement to anyone in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In Zenica, no, I never gave a statement to anyone in Zenica, except when the representatives from this Tribunal came to look for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with a commission that was set up to take care of the refugees from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was registered with the local commune, the one where I arrived, and this is where I received food, but I had no other contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, ma'am. We have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't, and the Prosecution will not need the witness any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness be released, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming to give evidence. You are released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would like to address the court concerning certain witness matters. We would like to ask that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
